articles.title: Speculative attack on rupee promoted foreign exchange measures: RBI
articles.summary: MUMBAI: The RBI’s curbs on foreign exchange trading were aimed at checking speculative bets against the rupee after the central bank found that around
articles.body: MUMBAI: The RBI’s curbs on foreign exchange trading were aimed at checking speculative bets against the rupee after the central bank found that around one-third of derivative trades were being cancelled or closed on the day they were entered into, governor Sanjay Malhotra said.In an interview with Moneycontrol published on Tuesday, Malhotra said the RBI had acted because speculative activity was amplifying currency volatility instead of serving genuine hedging needs. “We observed excessive volatility and one-sided bets that were preventing market forces from determining the rupee’s true value,” he said.The RBI announced a series of measures on Oct 10 after the rupee came under sustained pressure, touching a record low of 96.96 against the dollar on Friday. The steps included supplying dollars directly to three state-run oil marketing companies, tightening rules for foreign exchange derivatives and introducing a Foreign Exchange Risk Reserve requirement for banks on qualifying transactions.Malhotra said genuine hedging typically involved maintaining a position for the duration of the underlying exposure. “If a participant has a genuine underlying requirement, such as an import payment, they will typically maintain the hedge for the reasonable duration of that exposure,” he said. The high rate of same-day cancellations and rebooking indicated “a significant speculative element in the forex derivatives market”.The RBI does not seek to defend a particular exchange rate but wants to ensure that market forces determine the rupee’s value without excessive volatility. “We have repeatedly said that we do not target any particular price level or band for the rupee,” Malhotra said. “Our effort has always been to ensure orderly movement in the currency and prevent excessive speculation.”The central bank’s concern is that one-sided positioning can distort price discovery, making currency movements less reflective of underlying demand and supply. Its measures seek to curb speculative activity while allowing the exchange rate to be determined by market forces.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: The Iran war is costing American households $2,000 each, Moody’s estimates
articles.summary: The deeply unpopular war in the Middle East continues to deliver economic shockwaves through Main Street America.
articles.body: The deeply unpopular war in the Middle East continues to deliver economic shockwaves through Main Street America. From $4 gas and 7% mortgage rates to surging airfares, the Iran war is significantly raising the cost of living for inflation-weary consumers ahead of the midterm elections. The conflict has cost US consumers about $265 billion since it started in late February, according to estimates from Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody’s Analytics. That equates to about $2,000 in higher costs for the average American household. “Many Americans have rightly connected the dots between the Iran War and the painfully high cost of living and thus want the war to end,” Zandi told CNN on Tuesday. Not only have consumer prices increased, but paychecks are not keeping up. Wage growth slowed in September to a five-year low. Real wages, adjusted for inflation, have declined almost every month since the Iran war started, prompting some consumers to dip into savings and rely on credit cards to get by. Higher fuel prices cost families $1,100 Energy is at the heart of the financial fallout. The Iran war paralyzed the Strait of Hormuz for months, preventing staggering amounts of crude oil, fuel and liquefied natural gas from exiting the Persian Gulf. Oil flows have rebounded through that narrow waterway but the cost to get crude out of the Persian Gulf has now also skyrocketed, raising the cost of everything from gasoline and diesel to jet fuel. Soaring energy prices – including higher home heating bills – have cost the typical family about $1,100 since the war started. At current prices, that tally is rising by about $50 per week, Zandi estimates. Diesel, the workhorse fuel that powers trucks, tractors and trains, remains near all-time highs. Gasoline prices have stabilized but they are still unusually high for this time of year, at $4.34 a gallon nationally, according to AAA. That’s up from $2.98 a gallon before the conflict started. Pump prices have been persistently high since the war began. Tuesday marked the 165th day this year with the national average at or above $4 a gallon, according to a CNN review of AAA data. That’s easily the most for any calendar year since AAA started tracking in 2000, surpassing the prior record of 158 in 2022 during the Biden administration, much of which was attributed to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. The only other year where gas prices topped $4 a gallon was in 2008, when they were at or above $4 a gallon for 48 days during the summer before Lehman Brothers imploded. Airlines jack up fares, fees President Donald Trump has in the past argued that higher gas and diesel prices are a small price to pay for keeping Iran from getting a nuclear weapon. “Mark Zandi is a Democrat donor who is frequently wrong – including predicting multiple recessions that never happened,” a White House spokesperson told CNN in a statement on Tuesday. “President Trump is rightfully ensuring that Iran, a country that for 47 years chanted ‘Death to America,’ can never have a nuclear weapon.” (Zandi was an economic adviser to GOP presidential nominee John McCain in 2008.) Skyrocketing jet fuel prices have slammed the airline industry. Airlines have responded by cutting some cheaper and less profitable routes, jacking up baggage fees and raising airfare. The cost of airfare was up by 23% year over year as of August, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The price of heating oil, which is very similar to diesel, has also spiked. Homes using heating oil are expected to pay 21% more for the fuel than last winter, according to the US Energy Information Administration. 7% mortgage rates Moody’s found that the second-biggest consumer hit from the Iran war is in the form of higher borrowing costs. Higher inflation prompted the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates for the first time in three years and contributed to a sell-off in the bond market that has sharply driven up bond yields. Those higher bond yields have brought average 30-year fixed rate mortgage rates to 7.4%, a nearly three-year high. The cost of carrying a credit card balance and getting a car loan have also increased. Moody’s estimates that higher interest rates have cost the typical household about $360. The military conflict itself has been costly, a price that is ultimately borne by taxpayers. The Pentagon told lawmakers in September that the Iran war has cost $45.1 billion, CNN has previously reported, citing sources familiar with the matter. That estimate, however, is not comprehensive as it does not include the cost to repair damaged US bases or buildings in the region. The financial costs from the Iran war likely help explain why consumer confidence is in a tailspin and why the war is so unpopular. Just 27% of Americans approve of Trump on the economy and 28% call economic conditions good, according to a September CNN poll.

articles.title: Karnataka to drop repeat GST notices in closed cases
articles.summary: Karnataka to withdraw repeat GST notices in already audited and closed cases; commercial taxes dept also plans earlier audit notices and reviews audit scope.
articles.body: Bengaluru: Karnataka’s commercial taxes department will take steps to withdraw fresh GST notices issued in cases that have already been audited and closed, if affected businesses bring them to its attention, Vipul Bansal, commissioner of commercial taxes in the Karnataka govt, said on Tuesday.The assurance followed complaints from industry representatives about repeat proceedings and short deadlines to respond to tax notices during an interaction with senior tax officials on reforms recommended by the 57th GST Council meeting.“Wherever such cases are brought to our notice, we will take consequent action of actually dropping those notices,” Bansal said, adding that instructions had already been issued to field officers.He acknowledged that notices had been sent to businesses whose cases were already closed. The department had used data analytics to identify cases for scrutiny, and the system became operational around the time the notices were issued, he said.Karnataka also aims to issue notices for audits planned in a financial year before the year begins, giving businesses more time to prepare. Bansal said the department was committed to implementing this.“We are systemically ready. We just need to put it in practice,” he said.Separately, Sanjay Mangal, member (GST) of the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC), said the board was examining whether central GST audits should cover a single financial year or multiple years.Industry representatives said audits spanning three or four years required extensive documentation, while businesses were given little time to respond. They also raised concerns over the invocation of Section 74 of the CGST Act, which deals with cases involving fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression of facts.Mangal said uniform guidelines on issuing notices would clarify the circumstances in which the provision should be invoked and address its unnecessary use in audit matters.The board would take an internal decision on “whether we have to go for a single year audit or multiple year audit”, he said.You use AI every day. articles.title: Diesel futures jump, signaling higher prices to come despite Trump’s Russia deal
articles.summary: Diesel futures traded sharply higher Tuesday, as doubts mounted that the Trump administration’s recent maneuvers to lower prices would make much of an impact.
articles.body: Diesel futures traded sharply higher Tuesday, as doubts mounted about the likely impacts of the Trump administration’s latest efforts to push prices down. U.S. diesel futures were up 5% by midday to their highest level in weeks. In Europe, diesel futures rose by about 3.8%, while gas futures spiked to levels not seen all year. A move higher in futures markets typically signals that prices will climb in the coming days. Already, the average nationwide price of diesel is up 70% since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28. The cost of unleaded gas has risen by more than 45% over that period. Crude oil prices, meanwhile, were mixed. Brent traded around $106 per barrel, while U.S. crude oil neared $95 per barrel. Both of those key energy benchmarks have risen around 70% since the start of the year. Gas and diesel prices are rising especially fast in parts of the country where President Donald Trump and Republicans can least afford to anger voters ahead of November’s midterm elections. “Absolutely stunning price spikes in wholesale diesel today,” Gulf Oil adviser Tom Kloza wrote Tuesday on X. “US retail diesel price record of $6.53/gal could be topped by the midterms.” “Up 18cts/gal Gulf Coast and East Coast; but up 28cts/gal in Southern California and 25-30cts/gal in Great Plains and Great Lakes,” he wrote. Patrick De Haan, the head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, wrote on X that “$6/gal diesel may be here to stay for now.” “Truckers and farmers not going to see any relief anytime soon,” he wrote. The broad spike higher in diesel futures came just days after Trump announced a controversial deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to increase diesel supplies in the United States by buying previously sanctioned Russian reserves. When Trump announced the deal, he said it would result in millions of metric tons of additional diesel for the world. While that may sound like a lot, analysts have since crunched the numbers and determined that, at best, the diesel in question would amount to less than two weeks’ worth of U.S. demand. Tuesday’s higher diesel futures are evidence of the market “clearly not believing that Russian oil is on the way,” Kloza said. The deal with Putin also required that the Trump administration suspend long-standing sanctions on Russian energy purchases. The sanctions were put in place after Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, and the decision to lift them until April has drawn widespread backlash both at home and abroad. Trump has also applied pressure to European allies in an effort to get them to release more of their diesel reserves. The president’s Oct. 2 announcement that Europe had bowed to the pressure and would release fuel temporarily cooled prices for a few days. But a lack of additional details about that release gradually erased any price relief. A subsequent statement from the International Energy Agency confirmed what traders had suspected: Europe would not be releasing any new diesel reserves, merely continuing to fulfill a pledge it made in March as part of a multinational effort to cap rising fuel prices. Trump also signed an executive order this month that sought to ease restrictions on an off-road formulation of diesel that is dyed red and not subject to federal gas taxes. But industry groups quickly warned truckers to avoid using “red dye” diesel without more information about how the taxes would work. As of Tuesday, it was unclear whether Trump’s red dye diesel order had any impact on domestic prices or supply.

articles.title: Wall Street mixed as bank earnings lift Goldman, Iran war and inflation weigh
articles.summary: Wall Street stocks traded mixed on Tuesday as investors assessed a fresh batch of corporate earnings, with strong results from major US banks offset by
articles.body: Wall Street stocks traded mixed on Tuesday as investors assessed a fresh batch of corporate earnings, with strong results from major US banks offset by concerns over market volatility, inflation and the economic fallout of the Iran war.The S&P 500 slipped 0.1 per cent, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 190 points, or 0.4 per cent, and the Nasdaq Composite declined 0.2 per cent. The moves came as the benchmark indexes remained close to their record levels, with investors weighing whether companies can sustain their profit growth amid rising borrowing costs and geopolitical uncertainty.Goldman Sachs shares recovered to trade 0.3 per cent higher after initially jumping more than 4 per cent following a stronger-than-expected quarterly profit. The bank benefited from robust equities trading, although revenue from its fixed income, currencies and commodities business fell 1 per cent from a year earlier.Chief executive David Solomon said the economy remained resilient despite several headwinds. "The economy continues to be very, very resilient despite some of the headwinds," he said, pointing to a strong technology investment cycle and a regulatory environment encouraging corporate activity.Banking activity faces late-quarter slowdownResults from JPMorgan Chase, Citigroup, Goldman Sachs and Wells Fargo indicated that the dealmaking and trading momentum seen in the first half of the year may have moderated towards the end of the third quarter. Executives cited volatile equity markets, rising bond yields and uncertainty surrounding the economic outlook as factors weighing on investment banking activity.JPMorgan said market turbulence had slowed dealmaking and affected bond trading, particularly during the second half of September. However, chief financial officer Jeremy Barnum said the pipeline of potential deals remained "very strong", with many transactions delayed rather than cancelled.Goldman Sachs chief Solomon also expressed optimism about future activity, saying the initial public offering (IPO) market remained in good shape despite a recent loss of momentum. Companies could postpone listings until market conditions improve, he said.Citigroup chief financial officer Gonzalo Luchetti reported softer investment banking activity during the quarter, while Wells Fargo finance chief Mike Santomassimo also pointed to a slowdown in September as benchmark bond yields rose sharply."There is no doubt that high interest rates and the threat of continued Fed hikes is weighing on trading and IB activity in a measurably negative vector," said Brian Mulberry, chief market strategist at Zacks Investment Management.Trading revenue supports bank earningsEquities trading remained a bright spot for major banks as clients adjusted their portfolios amid uncertainty over interest rates and rising energy prices. JPMorgan reported a 15 per cent increase in revenue from its markets division in the third quarter compared with a year earlier, while equities markets revenue surged 49 per cent.Goldman also exceeded analysts' profit expectations, supported by stronger equities trading linked to volatility surrounding the Middle East conflict. Its fixed income, currencies and commodities business, however, recorded a year-on-year decline in revenue.JPMorgan shares rose 0.1 per cent after fluctuating between gains and losses, while Wells Fargo fell 1.8 per cent following weaker-than-expected revenue despite beating profit estimates. Citigroup shares also declined, while Goldman Sachs ended in positive territory.JPMorgan chief executive Jamie Dimon flagged elevated asset prices, persistent inflation, higher interest rates and geopolitical tensions as risks to the economic outlook. "These forces may be manageable, but we remain prepared for a wide range of outcomes," he said.Despite these concerns, bank executives said consumers and corporate borrowers remained resilient, with limited signs of deterioration in credit quality. Santomassimo said Wells Fargo was not seeing indications of significant financial stress among borrowers.Markets weigh earnings against wider risksBeyond the banking sector, technology stocks remained under pressure amid concerns about valuations and competition in the artificial intelligence industry. Micron Technology fell 5.1 per cent after reports that Chinese memory-chip maker CXMT was making advances that could challenge established players, including Micron, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. South Korea's Kospi index dropped 5.5 per cent.Bumble shares surged 56.2 per cent after the dating-app company agreed to a $1.3 billion all-cash buyout by Ithaca Holdings.In the bond market, the yield on the US 10-year Treasury eased to 5.22 per cent from 5.24 per cent late Friday, while oil prices declined. Brent crude fell 0.5 per cent to $106.11 a barrel as uncertainty over the Iran war continued to influence energy markets.The broader earnings outlook remains strong, with analysts forecasting nearly 30 per cent year-on-year profit growth for S&P 500 companies in the third quarter, according to FactSet. However, investors remain focused on whether corporate results can justify elevated stock valuations amid inflationary pressures, rising bond yields and geopolitical risks.Chris Kotowski, an analyst at Oppenheimer & Co, cautioned that much of the banks' earnings outperformance appeared to be concentrated in equities trading, raising questions about whether the gains could be sustained.You use AI every day. articles.title: Tier-2 cities outpace metros in digital credit use, trust remains hurdle: Report
articles.summary: Tier-2 cities lead India’s digital credit use, with 60% using BNPL vs 45% in metros; report flags trust, transparency and settlement delays as key hurdles.
articles.body: BENGALURU: India’s smaller cities are emerging as bigger users of digital credit than metros, even as consumers remain far more comfortable using payment apps to make payments than to borrow money, a new study has found.About 60% of respondents in Tier-2 cities have used Buy Now, Pay Later (BNPL) services, compared with 45% in metros and 52% in Tier-3 cities. Yet, 64% of urban respondents have never formally applied for digital credit through an app, pointing to a gap between the growing use of checkout financing and formal digital borrowing.The findings are part of the third edition of How Urban India Pays, a study by Pahlé India Foundation in partnership with Amazon Pay. The study surveyed 5,149 consumers across 100 cities and 1,054 merchants across 20 states.Rajiv Kumar, chairman of Pahlé India Foundation, attributed the higher adoption in smaller cities to unmet demand for formal credit. Traditional borrowing channels remain harder to access in these markets, particularly for consumers who lack the documentation required by banks, he said.“There is a demand for credit, unfulfilled demand for credit which digital credit is actually filling in,” Kumar told TOI.Vikas Bansal, CEO of Amazon Pay India, said rising aspirations among younger consumers were also driving borrowing in smaller cities. Digital platforms, he said, were reaching people who had previously had limited access to credit.Another finding was the higher adoption among salaried women. About 66.5% of salaried women surveyed had used BNPL or EMI products, compared with 59.3% of salaried men. Bansal described this as an encouraging sign of credit reaching segments that have historically been underserved.The study also challenged the perception that digital borrowing is largely driven by discretionary consumption. Around 27% of respondents said they had used digital credit to purchase work equipment or tools, 24% to start or expand a business or side income, and 22% for education or skilling.However, trust continues to constrain adoption. While awareness of digital credit products averaged 88%, usage averaged just 31% across the five products studied. Consumers rated their payment apps 3.98 out of five for making payments, but only 3.10 for borrowing.Bansal said the industry needed to simplify lending terms, improve transparency and strengthen consumer protection. “What I see is what I get,” he said, describing the assurance borrowers should have about interest rates, repayment conditions and other charges.He said the industry must also improve grievance redressal so that consumers become as comfortable borrowing digitally as they are making payments.The report also examined the merchant side of digital payments. While 80.6% of surveyed merchants expressed openness to digital payments, 72.1% of those reporting hesitation cited settlement delays as a concern.He also described the ongoing festive season as “historic” for Amazon Pay, saying Pay Later users and EMI transactions had doubled, while credit card activity was six times its usual run rate.You use AI every day. articles.title: Vance announces plan to use wartime authority to boost fuel production at Texas refinery
articles.summary: The Trump administration will use wartime authority to augment fuel production at a refinery in Texas, Vice President JD Vance announced on Tuesday. The move comes as high energy prices are putting a strain on the economy and are becoming a political liability ahead of the midterms. “I am pleased to announce that the Trump…
articles.body:
The Trump administration will use wartime authority to augment fuel production at a refinery in Texas, Vice President JD Vance announced on Tuesday. The move comes as high energy prices are putting a strain on the economy and are becoming a political liability ahead of the midterms.

“I am pleased to announce that the Trump administration, working with the refinery at Delek, has used the Defense Production Act and we’re going to expand the refinery right here in Tyler, Texas,” Vance said during a Texas rally.

“We want millions of gallons of commercial-grade and military-spec fuel to come out of this refinery, in addition to what it’s already producing,” Vance told the crowd.

The Defense Production Act gives the president the authority to increase the production of certain items to advance national security.

It’s unclear whether the use of the Defense Production Act will go beyond just this one refinery. The Hill has reached out to the White House for additional comment.

The announcement comes as gasoline and diesel prices remain high, averaging about $4.34 and $6.28 per gallon respectively on Tuesday, according to AAA .

Asked last week about the potential for the wartime authority to bring down prices in general, Andy Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates, was skeptical that it would do much to immediately improve the situation.

“Refineries that are currently in operation are already making as much diesel as they possibly can,” Lipow told The Hill last week. “There’s very little that the administration can do today to get more diesel fuel out of the refineries that are already in operation.”

“Your choice is: you can send more money to the refineries that are in operation so they can make investments to produce more diesel months and years down the road or you can see if there’s an opportunity to restart some of the refineries that have been recently shut down or you can build new refineries,” Lipow continued.

Prices are high as the war in Iran has driven up oil costs and weakened energy infrastructure in the Middle East and Ukraine has targeted Russian refineries as those two countries remain at war.

articles.title: Most say Trump more interested in his wealth than helping people like them: Survey
articles.summary: Most Americans say President Trump is more interested in his own wealth than helping people similar to them, according to a new poll. An Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll found that 56 percent of respondents described Trump’s overall prioritization of “his personal business interests” as “a lot” during his second term. Nineteen…
articles.body:
Most Americans say President Trump is more interested in his own wealth than helping people similar to them, according to a new poll.

An Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll found that 56 percent of respondents described Trump’s overall prioritization of “his personal business interests” as “a lot” during his second term.

Nineteen percent described the president’s overall prioritization of his personal business interests as “some” during his second round in the White House, while 12 percent and 11 percent said his overall prioritization of his business interests was “only a little” or “not at all,” respectively.

The poll also found that 11 percent of respondents described the president’s overall prioritization of “people like me” in his second presidential stint as “a lot,” while 18 percent described his overall prioritization of people like themselves during his second term as “some.”

Seventeen percent in the poll described Trump’s overall prioritization of people like themselves as “only a little” for his second term, while 51 percent said his overall prioritization of people similar to them was nonexistent.

The poll comes amid rocky political territory for the president and the GOP, with the Iran war nearing the eight-month mark and concerns about the cost of living sagging Trump’s approval numbers

The war in Iran has driven up energy costs thanks to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for the oil industry.

According to AAA, the average price of a gallon of diesel in the U.S. was about $6.28 on Tuesday afternoon, up from about $3.65 last year at the same time. The average price of a gallon of regular gas in the U.S. on Tuesday afternoon was about $4.34, up from about $3.08.

A late June financial disclosure from Trump revealed he accrued over $2 billion via various channels last year.

The AP-NORC poll took place from Sep. 24 to 26, featuring 2,140 people and a margin of sampling error of plus or minus 2.9 percentage points.

articles.title: CVS to pay $315M settlement over allegations of illegally filling opioid prescriptions
articles.summary: The Justice Department (DOJ) announced Tuesday that CVS Health has agreed to pay $315 million to settle lawsuits alleging the company illegally filled prescriptions for opioids and other controlled substances. The settlement resolves a lawsuit first filed in 2019 by former CVS employee Hillary Estright in 2019 under the whistleblower provision of the False Claims…
articles.body:
The Justice Department (DOJ) announced Tuesday that CVS Health has agreed to pay $315 million to settle lawsuits alleging the company illegally filled prescriptions for opioids and other controlled substances.

The settlement resolves a lawsuit first filed in 2019 by former CVS employee Hillary Estright in 2019 under the whistleblower provision of the False Claims Act, which allows private parties to sue on behalf of the U.S. It also settles the ensuing 2024 complaint that the federal government fi le d against CVS Health.

Allegations against the pharmacy chain included claims that it knowingly filled prescriptions for controlled substances that had no legitimate medical purpose, were not valid or were not issued through common professional practices. CVS Health’s corporate performance metrics allegedly encouraged these actions to enhance profit.

The settlement agreement does not serve as an admission of guilt by CVS Health or a reversal of the federal government’s argument that there were well-founded claims against the company.

“Today’s settlement requires CVS to implement additional safeguards to ensure that prescriptions for opioids and other controlled substances are dispensed only when medically appropriate,” DOJ Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate said in a statement.

Shumate continued, “The remedial measures in this agreement — including proactive monitoring of opioid prescribing patterns — will provide critical protections for patients and federal healthcare programs. The Department of Justice will continue to take steps to prevent the unlawful dispensing of opioids.”

Several other major retailers have agreement to opioid-related settlements in recent years including Walgreens and Kroger, as well as Walmart this past August . CVS previously agreed to pay $4.9 billion to states and other political subdivisions after facing over 3,000 individual lawsuits in 2022.

CVS Health maintains that it disagrees with the federal government’s allegations.

“Our more than 27,000 CVS pharmacists do their part to help keep America healthy and are highly trained in the safe and appropriate use of all medications. We’ve implemented best-in-class and first-of-their-kind programs to help our pharmacists make the best decisions on behalf of patients,” CVS Health said in a statement Tuesday.

“We strongly disagree with the claims made in this case, and our settlement with the DOJ admits no wrongdoing. We’re pleased to move forward and put this litigation behind us,” the company added.

articles.title: Scientists urge tighter AI controls to prevent global cyber risks
articles.summary: Call comes amid polls casting doubts on political leaders’ ability to manage AI risks as US midterm elections near.
articles.body:
A group of more than 300 scientists from around the world is calling for urgent changes to how artificial intelligence is developed and deployed amid growing concerns about its unpredictable behaviour.

The letter, released on Tuesday and signed by researchers representing universities and research institutes in 32 countries, warned that failures to follow basic cybersecurity practices could lead to damage to critical infrastructure.

Many recent incidents in which AI models escaped secure environments could have been prevented with stronger security systems, the scientists said.

They recommended that organisations developing and testing advanced AI systems capable of carrying out cyberattacks do so in more tightly controlled environments, including “air-gapped” systems that are not connected to the internet.

The letter comes amid growing concerns about AI’s capabilities and its potential impact on everyday users. On Monday, Anthropic warned that its AI models could soon be capable of creating self-spreading malware that could affect everyday internet-connected devices, including smart TVs, security cameras and smart appliances such as ovens.

The report found that AI systems could identify unfamiliar devices without human intervention. The company, led by Dario Amodei, warned that smaller AI models could be capable of carrying out autonomous attacks by the end of the year.

The malware could also be difficult to contain because it might take days to infect a device and could spread across multiple machines rather than remain concentrated in a single, controlled location.

Taking control of internet-connected devices can have immediate consequences. In France, for example , hackers compromised cooling systems across hundreds of supermarkets, raising temperatures and causing more than $220,000 in damage.

Meanwhile, Axios news organisation reported on Friday that Anthropic, OpenAI and other major AI company executives are privately preparing for the possibility of a catastrophic AI-related incident that could disrupt access to major financial services, the internet and potentially critical infrastructure such as water and power systems. Several industry insiders believe a major incident could occur within the next six months to a year, it said.

The scientists also called for more safeguards, including the creation of an international organisation to establish a set of best practices for AI alignment and containment along with timely reporting of incidents.

One of the signatories, David Lie, a professor at the University of Toronto’s Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, said his concerns began after OpenAI’s AI agents bypassed controls and hacked into servers at the tech company Hugging Face .

“One is that OpenAI, in setting up its test environment, didn’t appreciate how capable its agents were,” Lie said.

“These were the AI agents that they were designing. Second is that the AI agents independently found each other and chose to collaborate on this attack, and third is that they also intentionally tried to deceive and mislead their human creators.”

The letter underscores growing public concern about AI, including in the lead-up to the US congressional midterm elections. A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll found that 57 percent of voters said President Donald Trump’s administration was not taking AI risks seriously enough, while 54 percent said the same of Congress.

An AP-NORC poll echoed those findings, with about 80 percent of respondents saying the government should keep AI under human control. Respondents also expressed little confidence in either party’s ability to manage the technology: 39 percent said neither Republicans nor Democrats could be trusted to do a good job of reining it in, while 23 percent expressed greater confidence in Democrats and 21 percent in Republicans.

articles.title: 'We are in a higher interest rate world in terms of inflation shock'
articles.summary: S&P global chief economist Paul Grunwald was in India and spoke to TOI about the inflation challenge, the China shadow on manufacturing and large tech
articles.body: S&P global chief economist Paul Grunwald was in India and spoke to TOI about the inflation challenge, the China shadow on manufacturing and large tech companies impacting bond yields. Excerpts:What is driving global growth amid the headwinds?It's mostly the AI revolution. People are doing historical analysis of big Investment waves, canals, railroads, and this is one of the biggest in terms of GDP. So it's a big positive demand shock that pushes up output and prices. The debt issuance by hyperscalers, which is a proxy for capex, is $800 billion this year. We're on the steepest part of the gradient of the path and it's going to keep rising to well over $1 trillion per year and then stay there for a while. Since we're at the steepest part right now, we are seeing a huge contribution to growth.Sitting in the US, how do you view India? What are the challenges and the risks for India?India comes up as the new fast growing emerging market. China's not in an emerging market anymore so the growth baton has clearly passed to India, which is very different from China. China has overcapacity in manufacturing and India has a little bit of everything. The question is what's the path to middle income, upper middle-income status over the next generation if that doesn't go through manufacturing. The Europeans, Americans, the Japanese, rest of east Asia have taken that path. This goes back to AI. Is it possible that services become as tradable as manufacturers? There are some examples with AI where you could start to trade, say, medical services. But the path has to have productivity. If you look at the way China's been developing, it's different from the way Japan and Korea did, where they moved up the manufacturing ladder. China is filling the entire spectrum. They don't appear to be releasing the lower end. That's blocking the countries below them from doing what China did. India has a big domestic market, unlike Bangladesh or Vietnam, which have to trade their way up.Globally, do you see inflation as a big risk? What's your view on bond yields and will this be a shallow rate increase cycle by central banks?Bonds yields are led by the US. The size of debt issuance by hyperscalers has gone from being very small to $800 billion this year. We used to tell stories of govt crowding out the private sector. Here the private sector is crowding out govt. If we think price pressures are structurally higher now, we need higher interest rates to get our inflation targets. That gets built into the long-end of the curve. A lot of the success of central banks over the last few decades was helped by China keeping prices down by joining the global economy. Inflation has been sticky, particularly in the US. So, we are in a higher interest rate world in terms of the inflation shock right now. Crude prices jumped to $120 and are now back to around $100, but diesel, gasoline and US jet fuels are elevated. Those are going in as input prices into firms and consumers and they're starting to leak out. We can see the upstream price pressures in the producer price indices. It will show up in margin compression for firms, which is not going to be good, or they pass it to consumers. That's why you're seeing a couple of notches of tightening by central banks.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Bank of America ordered to pay historic $1.2 billion fine over alleged sanctions and anti-money laundering violations
articles.summary: The fine is the third-highest penalty ever issued by the Treasury Department, which found that the bank failed to report billions in suspicious transactions.
articles.body: Bank of America was ordered Tuesday to pay $1.2 billion to the Treasury Department, which said it violated anti-money laundering and sanctions laws. The penalty is the third largest ever issued in Treasury history, the agency said. As part of that total, the bank was ordered to pay $750 million to the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the largest fine it has ever levied. “Today’s actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement. As the second-largest bank in the country, Bank of America has more than 70 million clients and processes about $4.5 trillion in payments for individual customers every year. In addition, the bank handles $450 trillion in payments for corporate customers, including payrolls, corporate credit cards and supplier payments. The Treasury Department said Bank of America “admits that it willfully violated” the Bank Secrecy Act and “failed to maintain” an anti-money laundering program that met minimum requirements under the law. The bank also admitted having failed to file mandatory Suspicious Activity Reports. “Bank of America failed to timely report to FinCEN over $5 billion dollars in suspicious transactions, with over $1 billion of this activity implicating national security-related and other priority illicit finance risks, including suspicious transactions indicative of Chinese Money Laundering Networks, fraud, and potential trade-based money laundering with a substantial nexus to the southwest border,” the Treasury Department said in a statement. FinCEN is the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, which combats money laundering, illicit financial activities and terrorist financing networks around the world. “Financial crime compliance is serious, and we are responsible for getting it right,” Bank of America said in a statement to NBC News. “We have invested billions of dollars in technology and dedicated thousands of employees to combat financial crime, and our team is far along with and committed to completing the work required to address the issues raised by our regulators.” “We will continue to support federal and local law enforcement across thousands of investigations and report hundreds of thousands of suspicious activity reports each year.” In addition to the FinCEN violations, the Treasury Department said Bank of America is also settling “its potential civil liability for 475 apparent violations of multiple sanctions programs” with the Office of Foreign Assets Control, which oversees sprawling U.S. sanctions. The company “processed millions of dollars in payments in apparent violation of sanctions programs targeting Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics, and global terrorism,” the Treasury Department said. Bessent said, “When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire U.S. financial system to significant illicit finance risks.” Bank of America will report its third-quarter earnings shortly before 7 a.m. ET Wednesday.

articles.title: Bank of America fined $1.2 billion by Treasury Department for money laundering and sanctions law violations
articles.summary: The US Treasury Department on Tuesday announced it was imposing a more than $1.2 billion fine on Bank of America, accusing the bank of violating anti-money laundering and sanctions laws.
articles.body: The US Treasury Department on Tuesday announced it was imposing a more than $1.2 billion fine on Bank of America, accusing the bank of violating anti-money laundering and sanctions laws. The bank, which is the second-largest in the US, failed to mitigate and report “priority national security risks, including Chinese Money Laundering Networks and illicit finance along the southwest border,” the Treasury Department said in its announcement. “When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire U.S. financial system to significant illicit finance risks,” said Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent in a statement. “Today’s actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institution[s] are not above the law,” Bessent added. CNN reached out to Bank of America for comment. The $1.2 billion fine is the third-largest ever imposed by the Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), following a record $3.4 billion fine against Binance in 2023 and a $1.3 billion penalty against TD Bank in 2024. Both of those fines were also accompanied by charges from the Justice Department, though there is no accompanying Justice Department action for the Bank of America fine. The second Trump administration has taken actions against big banks for the practice of “debanking,” including through executive orders. Earlier this year, President Donald Trump also filed a $5 billion personal lawsuit against JPMorgan Chase, alleging that the country’s biggest bank closed his account for political reasons. However, the fine against Bank of America is the largest anti-money-laundering penalty the Trump administration’s Treasury Department has imposed on a major bank. As part of the total fine, $750 million will go to the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) as a civil penalty, making it the largest OCC penalty in history. As part of the settlement, Bank of America admitted that it willfully failed to have proper safeguards in place and failed to report suspicious activity, the Treasury Department said. Bank of America failed to respond in a timely and meaningful way to red flags involving suspicious customers, including those with ties to narcotics trafficking, even after compliance personnel escalated concerns, Treasury said. As a result, the bank, which processed more than $9 trillion in transactions last year, failed to report over $5 billion in suspicious activity. CNN learned that Bank of America’s sanctions-screening filter had a design flaw that prevented it from appropriately prioritizing certain potentially prohibited transactions. Specifically, when a transaction matched an individual’s name and date of birth on the US Treasury Department’s sanctions list, the bank’s system did not flag the transaction as high priority. The Treasury Department maintains a list of thousands of individuals and entities, including terrorists, narcotics traffickers, and companies subject to sanctions, whose assets may be blocked and who are generally prohibited from conducting transactions with US persons or entities. These breakdowns can cause harm to US sanctions programs, including the country’s Iran and counter-narcotics programs, which was the case with Bank of America, CNN learned. Dennis Kelleher, the CEO of Better Markets, which advocates for tougher regulations against banks, said in a statement that the $1.2 billion fine was small compared to Bank of America’s revenue. “Banks don’t break laws; people do, and until those people – including most importantly executives and supervisors – are personally and meaningfully punished by firings, prosecution, fines and being barred from employment in the industry, these crimes are not going to be stopped,” Kelleher said. Bank of America’s stock (BAC) fell more than 2.5% in after-hours trading after the fine was announced. The bank is expected to report quarterly earnings on Wednesday. “The OCC and FinCen are sending a message to BoA and to all banks — if you don’t fix the problem quickly they’ll be a big fine,” said Aaron Klein, the former deputy assistant secretary for economic policy at the Department of Treasury under President Barack Obama. “The OCC and FinCen have a lot of penalties they could impose beyond money — they can essentially fire people not just from BoA but from the entire business of banking.” “Everything the OCC is asking BoA to do to have a stronger anti-money laundering compliance program costs money, reducing the banks’ profit,” Klein added. CNN’s Matt Egan contributed to reporting.

articles.body:
Most see lawmakers as out of touch on spending

An overwhelming majority of voters believe current members of Congress are out of touch with their constituents’ monthly spending habits , even as both parties make affordability a central pitch to key voting blocs.

An exclusive NewsNation/Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) poll released Tuesday found that 86 percent of respondents believed their current congressmember or senator couldn’t accurately guess what they spend in a month, with 55 percent saying they thought lawmakers would guess too low while the other 31 percent expected lawmakers to guess too high.

Only 14 percent said they believed their lawmakers understood their monthly spending — underscoring the troubles Republicans face as the party in power as the Trump administration looks to quickly ameliorate inflation and cost of living issues before Election Day.

“When you ask [people] how they’re feeling about the economy, they don’t feel like things are getting better ,” Geoffrey Skelley, DDHQ’s chief elections analyst, told The Hill.

“They feel like things are getting worse, and considering [President] Trump was elected … in large part, to address economic challenges, I think that is also not helping the GOP,” he noted.

The full results of the poll will be discussed Tuesday night on “Decision Desk 2026 Have Your Say: A NewsNation Town Hall” hosted by NewsNation’s Chris Cuomo.

Rahm Emanuel , former White House chief of staff; Stephen A. Smith, broadcaster and commentator; and Steve Bannon, former Trump strategist, will discuss what they see in the numbers during the Cuomo Town Hall.

articles.title: What’s fueling inflation? Fuel.
articles.summary: Inflation in America is being powered by diesel.
articles.body: Inflation in America is being powered by diesel. The price of the fuel, used by farmers and truckers, is up more than 75% since the start of the Iran war in late winter. Diesel costs have become a particular concern for economists, who say that higher diesel fuel costs trickle down into “just about everything.” And the final government inflation report before November’s pivotal midterm elections will likely reflect how much of a headache it’s become for businesses and consumers. The Bureau of Labor Statistics is set to release its September consumer price index report at 8:30 a.m. Wednesday. It’s expected to show the annual rate of inflation rose to 3.7% from 3.4%, according to a survey of economists from Dow Jones. From August to September, prices are expected to have risen by 0.6%. The monthly jump, if confirmed, would also be one of the largest in years. Since August, oil prices have risen to more than $105 per barrel from about $80. The price of regular gas, which most consumers buy, also remains elevated by more than 45% since late February, when the Iran war was launched. As early voting kicks off this week, a higher inflation reading would come at a precarious moment for Republicans defending majorities in the House and Senate. Polls consistently find that inflation and the high cost of living are top issues this year for voters in both parties. Higher diesel prices this summer and fall have hit agricultural states like Kansas, Iowa and Texas especially hard. Long viewed as Republican strongholds, all three states have Democrats outperforming in Senate races with campaigns focused on the high cost of living. In response to the outcry over the high cost of gas and diesel, President Donald Trump has pulled several policy levers in recent weeks aimed at pushing down prices. But so far, none of them has made much of a dent. The Trump administration has pressured G7 allies to release more diesel stocks, issued an order to allow more widespread use of tax-free diesel, and announced a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin that Russia release some diesel supplies and drop some of its export restrictions. The latest action has drawn global backlash after Trump also eased some sanctions on Russia in order to facilitate the Russian diesel deal. Core concerns Consumers’ wages are still lagging behind the rate of inflation. As of September, wage growth was 3% and has not grown faster than inflation since March. Still, despite the pressure on prices and wages, consumers continue to spend. The CEOs of the nation’s largest banks on Tuesday reported that consumers remain spending at a steady pace. “While various headwinds, most recently higher energy prices, and tighter monetary policies have been challenging, the global economy has held up remarkably well in the U.S.,” said Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser. “While much has been made of the AI boom, the consumer is still driving much” of the economy’s momentum, she added. “Our data shows that our consumer and business customers are doing well,” said Wells Fargo CEO Charlie Scharf. JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon said the economy “continued to be fueled by strong business investment and ongoing consumer spending” over the last three months. Core inflation, which is more closely watched by the Federal Reserve and which strips out food and energy prices, is expected to rise as well, to 2.5%. If confirmed, that would be its highest level since June. One key sector fueling higher core inflation is airfare. “Airfares remain the core category most directly affected by higher oil prices,” said economists at Morgan Stanley. “Airfare CPI is already up 23% y/y, which raises the question of how much further prices can increase.” They noted that jet fuel prices have risen 90% since this time last year, “and typically account for roughly 20-30% of airline operating costs.” As a result, “Airlines may already be approaching full pass-through of the increase in fuel costs to consumers.” iPhones and interest rates Another major consumer item that could impact September’s inflation rate: pricier iPhones. Apple’s latest iPhone began selling on Sept. 12, and Morgan Stanley’s economists said “price increases were generally in the 10%-14% range across models.” “Given Apple’s roughly 50% share of the U.S. smartphone market,” this could translate into what they said could be a small upside impact on overall inflation. But while these higher iPhone prices are likely contributing to September’s inflation, they are also the product of inflation earlier his year — inflation that traces back to the ever-expanding buildout of AI data centers. The race to build data centers and chips for AI has triggered a scramble for memory, in particular. Given that the supply of memory chips is limited, prices have soared at an unprecedented pace. In June, Apple told NBC News that it has “never seen a component price increase this much, this quickly.” Economists at Goldman Sachs also expect to see a jump in September in other key consumer categories. “We expect a pickup in autos inflation, reflecting a 0.5% increase in used car prices, a 0.2% increase in new car prices, and a 0.2% increase in the car insurance category,” they wrote in a note. Wednesday’s data could also “determine whether the Fed’s next hike is imminent, or simply still ahead,” said economists at UBS. Already, the central bank has interest raised rates once this year to try to slow inflation. A number of top Fed officials have also spoken about the need to raise rates even higher. “If the economic data continue to come in as expected, I anticipate additional hikes to support a timelier return of inflation to our two percent goal,” said Federal Reserve governor Christoper Waller on Thursday. “But there is some flexibility about when those hikes will occur.” The Fed is expected to raise rates one more time this year, most likely in December. But an inflation reading on Wednesday that comes in hotter than expected could increase that urgency and lead to a pre-Election Day rate hike at the central bank’s Oc. 27-28 meeting.

articles.body: OpenAI discovered a “sophisticated recording device” in one of its offices planted by an employee who has been arrested, the company said Tuesday. The employee, who has since been dismissed by the company, is a Saudi national and has been identified by the US Department of Justice as 35-year-old Abdulrahman Alfozan. The device was discovered on September 30 during a regular sweep of a conference room where the device was found inserted into a USB port on the back of a television screen and “concealed in toilet paper,” according to the DOJ. OpenAI has determined the device was in the conference room for about two days before it was discovered. Alfozan, who had been an engineer on the product team since July 2025 the DOJ said, was arrested on October 9 and remains in federal custody. CNN has reached out to Alfozan for comment. OpenAI said the device was for monitoring audio, had advanced encryption, and a mechanism for transferring data designed to evade monitoring. Alfozan had been seen on security cameras accessing the meeting room, where “highly confidential” discussions took place. The DOJ said a backpack belonging to Alfozan was found to have other similar recording devices, and OpenAI said they have evidence he intended to deploy more recording devices throughout their offices. “At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data,” OpenAI said in a statement. “We take protecting our technology, data, and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance.” The DOJ alleged that Alfozan used a “productivity tool” to find information about OpenAI’s meeting rooms, calendars and the locations of its leadership. A chatbot associated with Alfozan’s wife was found to have submitted prompts about building an encrypted audio recording device. A LinkedIn page listed under Alfozan’s name showed previous positions at Meta as a senior systems engineer for around five years, as well as a company called Nash. The profile says that Alfozan attended the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and University of California, Berkeley. He’s also a partner in Raed, a Saudi based venture capital firm. CNN has reached out to the firm for comment. In a statement, U.S. Attorney Craig Missakian said the protection of US technology companies is “a matter of national security.” This is a developing story and will be updated.
